sections.heading: Claims
sections.text:
The article's central, repeated finding, stated as a section heading and then demonstrated with an ATC worked example (comparing two Arrival Manager configurations — one giving controllers a low-level advisory they could act on flexibly, one giving a precise directive):

> "The highest possible level is not always the best level... A lower level of automation might be better than no automation."

On why full substitution of the human is rare in practice, from the same piece:

> "Only in very few cases automation is about completely replacing the human... [even where] 'the pilot is no longer in the loop'... the role of the crew remains a central one."

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Not a controlled experiment — a practitioner synthesis for EUROCONTROL's HindSight safety magazine, applying the Level of Automation Taxonomy (LOAT, developed by the author and B. Feuerberg for the SESAR "Good Practices for HP Automation Support" project) to 26 real automated functionalities drawn from both ground (ATC) and aircraft systems — including the TCAS Resolution Advisory/autopilot interaction, Medium Term Conflict Detection tools, and two Arrival Manager configurations — and reports four qualitative findings from that classification exercise.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- **The underlying LOAT taxonomy's development base is modest and stated plainly:** "26 examples of automated functionalities, from both ground and aircraft-related systems" — a purposive sample assembled for one SESAR deliverable, not a systematic survey of all ATC/flight-deck automation.
- **This is a secondary, practitioner-facing application of Sheridan & Verplank (1978) and Parasuraman, Sheridan & Wickens (2000), not a new primary theoretical contribution** — the article cites both explicitly as its foundation and extends their four-function framework into a more granular per-function level count (LOAT: 5/5/6/8 levels across the four stages) for the ATC/aviation domain specifically.
- **Findings are illustrative case comparisons, not statistically powered results** — e.g., the AMAN comparison is a single field observation about controller preference under one airspace's specific terrain/geography constraints, presented as an instructive example rather than a generalizable effect size.
- **Author's institutional position is disclosed and relevant to weighing the source**: Dr. Save is a Safety and Human Factors R&D expert at Deep Blue, a EUROCONTROL/SESAR contractor — this is applied aviation-safety consulting work published in an EUROCONTROL practitioner venue (HindSight), not an independently peer-reviewed academic journal; treat it as well-grounded applied commentary building directly on the peer-reviewed Parasuraman et al. model, not as an independent primary empirical study.
